To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pigeons' recall of relational stimuli in a delayed matching-to-sample task depends upon the complexity of the discrimination.

the rate of decrement of stimulus control over time is the same for single- and relational-discrimination procedures but that the initial level of control is greater for single than for relational discriminations, and that initial levels of control for single discriminations are greater for easier than for more difficult discriminations.

the rate at which pigeons forget stimuli presented in a symbolic matching-to-sample task is not affected by whether the stimuli are single or relational, but is affected by the relative discriminability of the stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the sample stimulus in the recall process.
the role that stimulus complexity plays in the acquisition and retention of information in memory.
the role of relational stimuli in the development of delayed recall for stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the recallability of relational stimuli is not a simple function of their complexity, but is a function of their discriminability.

the rate at which recall decreases with increasing delay since presentation is the same for both single and relational stimuli, but initial levels of performance differ, and that the rate of recallability decrement is independent of discrimination difficulty.
recall for single and for relational stimuli is a function of discrimination difficulty.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pigeons' memory for stimuli is limited to a few minutes and is affected by the complexity of the stimuli and the difficulty of the discrimination.
recall functions are not affected by stimulus complexity but by the ease with which the stimuli can be discriminated.
recall for stimuli differing in discriminability is affected both by the initial level of recallability and by the rate at which this decreases with increasing delay since the sample presentation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found that pigeons could learn to use a relational rule in a visual discrimination task, but that the pigeons’ performance was not perfect.
the rate of decay in recallability is the same regardless of the difficulty of the discrimination.
the relational discrimination is more difficult to acquire than the single discrimination, but the recallability of the stimuli is not different.
